Like many people, I started on Ubuntu. Now I own an old laptop and I run xubuntu because it's small enough to keep on a cd and light enough to run on an old laptop. I've experimented with arch and I like the community and pacman and the arch wiki. Problem is, it's hard to install, and I'm worried about having to constantly work on my laptop more when arch is installed. It's just arch forces me to actually customize things, like trying out a new desktop environment and the like. Any thoughts?
Should I switch from xubuntu to arch?

As long as you can follow the guide, the basic installation and setup shouldn't take more than a few hours. You don't have to do a lot of customization right away, you can start with Xfce and whatever software you're used to and switch things up later if you feel like it. Once you have everything ready, Arch doesn't necessarily require any more maintenance than xubuntu, just run pacman -Syu every now and then and that's pretty much it.

What purpose are you trying to fill? That will determine your choices.

If you just want a light weight, easy to use distro, then I would migrate to the experimental version of Debian. Its super light weight, fully featured, but still very familiar for a Xubuntu user.

Or, you could just stay with Xubuntu. If it works, don't fix it.
Try it, it'll be hard only the first few times then it just becomes a matter of following the steps and installing what you need.

Arch is cool if you want to slim down your system for performance. If you don't like something like network manager polling constantly and making your audio stutter for example, it is a little easier on arch to move away from the defaults the distros give you.

But having debs or rpms often makes it easier to get your printers and stuff working.

The only reason to install arch (or gentoo for that matter) is if you want the best optimization for your hardware. It really only makes sense in 3 cases: a) you got an older computer that you want to run linux on without any of the overhead, b) you want to make a computer as fast as possible for specific games, or c) you really want to learn how everything works underneath.

To get everything to work, its just a lot of reading and googling. I wouldn't say its hard, its just more work and time intensive and you just basically try stuff and google errors.

Other then that, the debian based distros just have more of a userbase, even though they are not bleeding edge, so it doesn't take much effort (relatively) to get stuff to work on them.
